title: Develop Shared Commitments, Political Alignment and Ownership
description: This Action includes guidance and tools to help national, subnational and city governments to jointly establish shared political commitment, collective ownership and long-term alignment required to support multilevel climate finance and implementation.
systemsLogic: Multilevel climate action starts with shared political commitment. Joint commitment processes can create a common mission, clarify roles across governance levels, and build the mandate, trust and institutional relationships needed for later stages of investment planning, finance mobilization, implementation and learning. In practice, they help move climate action from isolated pledges toward coordinated, network-based governance.

pathways.title: Joint Political Commitments, Dialogues and Coalitions
pathways.whatItIs: Joint political commitment dialogues and coalition mechanisms provide a recurring process through which national, subnational and city governments can establish a shared vision, align climate priorities and create long-term coalitions for coordinated climate action and investment. They help create a collaborative governance arrangement to clarify institutional roles and responsibilities, aligns actors around a common mission, and establishes a shared mandate for implementation of climate projects.

implementationGuidance.content: The process starts by creating a strong political mandate and mapping the local system, so the commitments reflect real conditions rather than generic targets.

illustrativeExamples.title: The Joint Commitment process of the Climate City Contracts (CCC)
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: The Joint Commitment process of the Climate City Contracts (CCC) demonstrates how joint political commitment can be turn...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Joint Commitment process of the Climate City Contracts (CCC) demonstrates how joint political commitment can be turned into a recurring multilevel governance arrangement rather than a one-off declaration. The contract process is built around a shared climate-neutrality mission and an annual cycle in which cities, Viable Cities and national agencies each make commitments, review progress and renew priorities. The city’s role is to gather the wider transition arena, which includes a space for collaboration, coordination and dialogue among public and private actors who need to help deliver the transition and connect local action to national support. The contract itself is structured in three linked parts — climate goals, a roadmap or portfolio of actions, and a climate investment plan — so political commitment is tied to implementation planning and financing. Through a joint commitment mechanism, the Climate City Contracts process is designed to work through a broader network of businesses, academia, civil society and public organizations, helping shift municipalities from traditional governance toward a more network-based model.

illustrativeExamples.title: Town Hall COPs are a strong emerging...
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Town Hall COPs are a strong emerging example of how multilevel dialogues and commitments can help bridge local implement...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Town Hall COPs are a strong emerging example of how multilevel dialogues and commitments can help bridge local implementation with national climate strategy and planning.  Launched by ICLEI Africa in 2025, the format gives local governments and communities a dedicated space to discuss climate goals, jointly review progress and identify next steps in line with national plans and global commitments. The Town Halls also bring in national government representatives (with national presence recorded at 60% of events) so local priorities could be heard directly and fed into NDC and NAP implementation. By October 2025, 18 Town Hall COPs were convened, engaging over 2000 participants, across six Sub-Saharan African countries. These participants ranged from mayors and national agency officials to the youth and civil society. The dialogues helped develop and surface over 300 local commitments. In South Africa, the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment became the first national government to recognise the model as a platform for inclusive national climate planning and local implementation of the NDC, Building on this endorsement, ICLEI Africa and the South African Local Government Association (SALGA) rolled out the Town Halls across the country to enable multilevel dialogues and subsequent commitments, which feed back into policy, implementation and reporting. Click here to know more about the Town Hall COPs.

transferability: Joint political commitment mechanisms can be adapted to different governance contexts by:

Develop a joint political commitment and dialogue process where cities and national agencies have the capacity to coordinate and sustain the commitment. In Sweden, the joint commitment process of the Climate City Contracts works because municipalities are powerful actors, the process is renewed annually, and the framework can be used to understand governing and supporting processes across local, regional, national and European levels.

Where local capacity is uneven, start with recurring multilevel dialogue, with an ambition to move towards a full CCC-like process. The Town Hall COPs in Africa show that a lighter, dialogue-based model can still generate commitments, national buy-in and policy inputs feeding into NDCs and NAPs.

Allow cities to enter at different readiness levels. Structure the process with mandatory commitments for all cities and optional commitments that cities can join based on their readiness, as shown by the Transition Arena model. That makes transferability stronger, because it gives countries a common floor while still allowing different cities to move at different speeds and with different tools.

Build from pioneer municipalities in context with low readiness levels. In contexts where national coordination exists unevenly or is not strong enough to sustain long-term joint commitments, a national government help build momentum by backing a few municipalities that are already willing to move ahead, then help them work as a cluster and share experience.

Aligning commitments with existing political and budgeting cycles so that political commitments become part of routine government decision-making. Periodic reviews can then be used to update commitments based on implementation progress and emerging political priorities.
Embedding regular review and renewal processes to maintain political ownership, strengthen accountability and adapt commitments as implementation progresses.
enablingConditions: A shared long-term mission or national strategy that provides a common direction for national and subnational governments while allowing flexibility in local implementation.
Political will of both national and local leadership, ensuring that political commitments are jointly owned and can be sustained beyond electoral cycles.
Clearly defined institutional roles and responsibilities so that each participating actor understands its contribution and accountability.

title: Assess Enabling Environments
description: This Action will provide foundational assessment tools to identify and improve the policy, fiscal, data and coordination conditions needed for national, subnational and city governments to plan, access and deploy urban climate finance. It will help users diagnose barriers to climate investment readiness, including gaps in financing architecture, intergovernmental transfers, subnational borrowing, data systems, coordination, private finance mobilization and project bankability. System Logic: Multilevel climate investment depends on enabling conditions across data, policy, budget and finance, and coordination. Assessing enabling environments can therefore help identify and improve the readiness of national, subnational and city governments to jointly plan investments, implement portfolios and pipelines, mobilize finance and build capacities. Enabling environments also shape the ability of private financial actors to identify, structure, finance and implement climate investment opportunities.

pathways.title: National and subnational enabling environments assessments
pathways.whatItIs: Assessment of enabling environments helps unpack the conditions that affect urban climate finance in specific national and subnational contexts. It examines climate policy, budget and finance, climate data, and vertical and horizontal coordination, then translates the findings into recommendations, reform priorities and, where relevant, roadmaps or blueprints for follow-up action. The national tool is aimed primarily at national officials, while the subnational tool is designed for cities and other subnational governments; the two are meant to be used together where possible so the enabling environment can be assessed across levels of government.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify key government partners and define the scope of the assessment, including the relevant government levels and institutions.

implementationGuidance.title: Collect evidence through policy and document review, interviews, focus groups and data inventory.

implementationGuidance.title: Translate the results into follow-up actions, including roadmaps or blueprints to address the identified gaps.

pathways.whyItIsNeeded: Multilevel climate investment depends on enabling conditions being in place across data, policy, budget and finance, and coordination — yet these are often weak, uneven or invisible to decision-makers, leaving national, subnational and city governments unsure where the readiness gaps lie. To this end, enabling environment assessments surface where those conditions fall short, consolidate them into a comparable readiness profile, and channel the findings into concrete reforms, so the diagnostic feeds directly into investment planning, finance mobilisation and implementation rather than remaining a standalone report.

illustrativeExamples.title: National Enabling Framework Conditions (EFC) Tools offer...
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: National Enabling Framework Conditions (EFC) Tools offer a practical way to assess a national government against four ke...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: National Enabling Framework Conditions (EFC) Tools offer a practical way to assess a national government against four key dimensions – policy, budget and finance, climate data, and vertical and horizontal coordination. These categories are further broken down into 16 sub-categories that include 64 assessment dimensions. The dimensions help identify priority areas for reform, and the process includes identifying stakeholders, collecting evidence, holding consultations, preparing results and identifying follow-up actions. The tool was piloted in India and Indonesia, making it a strong EMDE reference for how national enabling conditions can be assessed and translated into reform.

illustrativeExamples.title: The India pilot (2024)
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: The India pilot (2024) illustrates how the national tool works in practice. The pilot was led by GIZ, alongside the Indi...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The India pilot (2024) illustrates how the national tool works in practice. The pilot was led by GIZ, alongside the Indian Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, the National Institute of Urban Affairs and The Energy Research Institute. It included a desk review with seven stakeholder interviews and two roundtables in New Delhi attended by more than 80 participants. The findings on the four dimensions included gaps in local institutional mandates, own-source revenues and borrowings, city-level climate data and coordination between state and local governments. Each gap points to a specific reform — broadening grants from the national finance commission to support climate action, for instance, or issuing city climate action plan guidelines under national missions. Another pilot in Indonesia runs the same tool with the national planning ministry (Bappenas) and pilot cities including Padang and Medan. By feeding directly into partners' capacity-building work with government stakeholders rather than sitting as a standalone report, both pilots turn the assessment into an input to reform. Click [here] to know more about the pilots.

illustrativeExamples.title: Subnational Enabling Framework Conditions (EFC) Tool mirrors...
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Subnational Enabling Framework Conditions (EFC) Tool mirrors the same logic as that of the national tool, but is adapted...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Subnational Enabling Framework Conditions (EFC) Tool mirrors the same logic as that of the national tool, but is adapted for a specific city, metropolitan area, state or region depending on context. It is organized around 49 dimensions in four categories and 13 sub-categories. The tool walks users through a similar workflow — define the scope, gather evidence through document review and interviews, convene workshops to validate findings, and then turn the results into roadmaps or blueprints.

transferability: The EFC Tools provide a standardised approach, but applying them in a new jurisdiction requires tailoring to context rather than direct replication:

Adapt the assessment methodology to context. Where subnational climate, fiscal and governance data are limited, lean on interviews and policy review — as the India pilot did with its desk review and seven stakeholder interviews — while reflecting the real intergovernmental relationships in play where mandates are unclear, and calibrating the access-to-finance analysis to the actual depth of local financial systems and intermediation.

Deploy the National and Subnational Tools together, so a new jurisdiction is assessed as a coherent multilevel system rather than at a single level in isolation, with the national baseline framing the subnational diagnosis, as in the India and Indonesia pilots.

Secure access to stakeholders and source documentation for the data-collection, inception and validation steps — the policies, budgets and officials the process depends on — much as the India pilot used its two New Delhi roundtables to confirm findings.

Ground the assessment in government ownership and existing planning and budget cycles, so its recommendations are taken up as live reforms; in India, the gaps mapped directly onto instruments already in use, such as Central Finance Commission grants and NMSH 2.0, rather than requiring new mechanisms.
Identify technical partners to run the workshops, interpret the scored dimensions and translate findings into roadmaps, as GIZ did alongside MoHUA, NIUA and TERI in the India pilot.
enablingConditions: Availability of governance, financial and climate-related data, since the depth of accessible data bounds what any assessment can conclude, and strengthening subnational climate data is itself one of the four EFC dimensions.
Institutional capacity and technical assistance to undertake the assessment and interpret findings — frequently a precondition rather than an optional add-on where in-house capacity is limited.
Coordination across national ministries, subnational governments and stakeholders, which the inception and final workshops are built to secure and which is itself a scored EFC dimension.
Political ownership and a mandate to act on findings, so recommendations are taken up rather than shelved — the reason the India pilot convened 80+ stakeholders in policy roundtables.

Alignment with existing policy, fiscal and financing frameworks, so reforms can be channelled through intergovernmental transfers, finance-commission grants and municipal budgeting rather than through entirely new mechanisms.

title: Institutionalize Multilevel Governance Frameworks and National Platforms
description: This section will include guidance and tools to help national, subnational and city governments to institutionalize long-term multilevel governance by building coordination capabilities, strengthening institutional arrangements and creating the investment and implementation capacities needed to sustain climate transitions.
systemsLogic: Institutionalizing multilevel climate investment is fundamentally about building long-term implementation capacity rather than creating one-off coordination mechanisms. Iterative coordination frameworks can help develop governance capabilities across institutions. These could be supported by nationally led coordination platforms capable of aligning governance, financing, project preparation, implementation actors and investment priorities across levels of government and the private sector, along with intermediary units for day-to-day coordination, monitoring, accountability and feedback loops. These arrangements also help strengthen institutional memory, leadership, trust, learning and feedback loops across organizations.

pathways.title: Overarching, Iterative Coordination Mechanisms
pathways.whatItIs: An overarching, iterative coordination framework provides the institutional architecture through which national, subnational and city governments, together with financial institutions, infrastructure providers, project developers and other implementation partners, can coordinate climate action and investment over the long term.

implementationGuidance.title: It operates through recurring cycles of joint planning, investment prioritisation, implementation, monitoring and learning, enabling stakeholders to continuously coordinate actions, address implementation barriers and refine priorities as circumstances evolve
implementationGuidance.content: It operates through recurring cycles of joint planning, investment prioritisation, implementation, monitoring and learning, enabling stakeholders to continuously coordinate actions, address implementation barriers and refine priorities as circumstances evolve

pathways.whyItIsNeeded: An iterative framework can help build long-term institutional relationships – strengthening implementation capacity and creating continuous feedback loops between planning, financing and delivery. Implementing such a framework can help governments sustain climate transitions over time, rather than having one-off coordination or consultations.

illustrativeExamples.title: Colombia's  Strategic Committee on Cities and Climate Change
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Colombia's  Strategic Committee on Cities and Climate Change illustrates how an overarching, iterative coordination fram...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Colombia's  Strategic Committee on Cities and Climate Change illustrates how an overarching, iterative coordination framework can support long-term multilevel climate governance. Co-hosted by the national government and WRI, the committee is not a one-off convening but the institutional architecture through which national authorities, subnational and city governments, and partners such as NGOs and funders coordinate climate action and investment over time. It operates through recurring cycles: a biannual forum brings these actors together to review city climate plans for alignment with national commitments such as Colombia's updated NDC and long-term strategy (E2050), identify active projects and synergies, prioritise high-impact and feasible measures, and connect them to enabling mechanisms — for example the Corridor of Climate Financing, a platform led by the National Planning Department that links climate projects to funders and provides support. By convening the same actors repeatedly rather than through one-off consultations, the framework builds long-term institutional relationships, strengthens implementation capacity and creates continuous feedback loops between planning, financing and delivery, helping the country address persistent political, financial and technical barriers and sustain its climate transition as circumstances evolve.

transferability: Adapting coordination frameworks and processes to the country's governance systems, enabling countries and cities to define governance relationships, supporting processes and coordination arrangements that reflect their own institutional context. In centralized systems, a national ministry could lead coordination, while decentralized may distribute coordination responsibilities across regional or state governments working alongside cities.
Building on existing coordination mechanisms, such as climate or NDC units, national platforms, subnational climate cells or sectoral coordination bodies, rather than creating parallel institutions.

Applying the coordination mechanisms progressively, where countries with limited institutional capacities may begin with simpler multistakeholder dialogues and progressively institutionalize recurring coordination processes as governance capabilities develop.
enablingConditions: Long-term political and institutional leadership to sustain collaboration, coordination and implementation across electoral and funding cycles.
Clearly defined governance relationships, roles and supporting processes that enable actors across governance levels to coordinate effectively within their own institutional context.
Regular coordination forums, learning processes and feedback mechanisms that enable actors to share knowledge, coordinate actions and continuously refine implementation.

pathways.title: National Platforms
pathways.whatItIs: In the context of CHAMP, national platforms are best understood as nationally owned and led initiatives for long-term coordination and implementation of climate action. Their purpose is to align political leadership, sectoral planning, finance and implementation around a shared national strategy, while creating a dedicated space for subnational governments, cities, development partners and other actors to work through priorities together. These platforms can be designed to bring urban and subnational priorities into the core of the process, so cities are not treated as downstream implementers but as co-shapers of priorities, pipelines and delivery arrangements. A useful way to think about them is as an enabling architecture for moving from fragmented, project-by-project action to a more programmatic, systemic approach.

implementationGuidance.title: National coordination platforms can be implemented as part of a...
implementationGuidance.content: National coordination platforms can be implemented as part of a phased, iterative process that moves from whole-of-government ownership and subnational engagement to program readiness, investment pipeline development, finance mobilization and adaptive implementation. This process could include:

implementationGuidance.title: Start with whole-of-government ownership and subnational entry points, where national leadership sets the mandate, while engagement with cities and regions brings urban priorities into the platform.
implementationGuidance.content: Start with whole-of-government ownership and subnational entry points, where national leadership sets the mandate, while engagement with cities and regions brings urban priorities into the platform.

implementationGuidance.title: Align sectoral priorities and planning across national and subnational climate goals and governance levels.
implementationGuidance.content: Align sectoral priorities and planning across national and subnational climate goals and governance levels.

implementationGuidance.title: Use the platform to support cities in developing local climate action plans and identifying project pipelines, mobilize technical assistance and enable financier matchmaking.

pathways.whyItIsNeeded: Cities and subnational governments often face misalignment with national climate and development priorities, limited entry points into decision-making, weak project pipelines, and fiscal and creditworthiness constraints that make climate finance hard to access. To this end, a national platform creates a space for local and national actors to align policies, pipelines and finance across levels of government so urban climate action can move from fragmented projects to a more programmatic delivery model.,

illustrativeExamples.title: Viable Cities
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Viable Cities demonstrates how a nationally anchored platform can turn climate ambition into an ongoing multilevel imple...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Viable Cities demonstrates how a nationally anchored platform can turn climate ambition into an ongoing multilevel implementation architecture rather than a one-off coordination exercise. In Sweden, Viable Cities works with 48 cities and six government agencies and coordinates the country’s participation in CHAMP. Through the Climate City Contract approach, Viable Cities helps align municipal commitments with national support, shared learning and implementation capacity. The platform’s value lies in that continuity – it connects local priorities to a national mission, creates a common framework for collaboration and implementation, and helps keep governance, planning and implementation moving together over time. Click here to know more about Viable Cities.

illustrativeExamples.title: CitiES 2030
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: citiES 2030 is a strong example of a nationally anchored, multilevel and multi-stakeholder coordination platform that he...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: citiES 2030 is a strong example of a nationally anchored, multilevel and multi-stakeholder coordination platform that helps turn climate mission goals into implementation support for cities. It brings together cities, public sector actors, private sector partners, academia, civil society and citizens, and it works across European, national and local levels within the EU Cities Mission and Adaptation Mission. The platform provides services for learning and capacity building, Climate City Contract development, and the implementation of interconnected project portfolios and multi-city collaboration. In Spain, that support has helped five cities submit their Climate City Contracts and receive the EU Mission Label, showing how a platform can connect national coordination with concrete city-level implementation. illustrativeExamples.title: Tanzania’s Integrated National Financing Framework (INFF)
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Tanzania’s Integrated National Financing Framework (INFF) is a useful example to illustrate how a nationally led platfor...
illustrativeExamples.fullText:
Tanzania’s Integrated National Financing Framework (INFF) is a useful example to illustrate how a nationally led platform can be adapted across levels of government when it is paired with local ownership, iterative strategy-building and robust international cooperation for public and private finance. Rolled out on the mainland and in Zanzibar, the process aligned financing and development planning, broke silos within the Ministry of Finance and Planning, and used pilot dialogues with LGAs to surface locally appropriate financing solutions and bankable projects. INFF has demonstrated visible early results in Tanzania. Zanzibar’s revenue collection system is now used by 10 of 11 regional administrations, Zanzibar launched a USD 450 million sovereign sukuk, Tanga issued a USD 20.5 million water green bond, four SDG-aligned corporate bonds totalled USD 380 million, a USD 60 million road infrastructure bond to was issued to empower local contractors. Further, Zanzibar’s redesigned SDG Investor Map helped mobilize USD 5.5 million. Moreover, in coordination with national government via multilevel dialogues, Tanzanian cities like Dodoma have started developing their own local frameworks targeting local challenges and opportunities, such as improving local revenues.

Click here to know more.

illustrativeExamples.title: CCFLA’s Urban-Inclusive Country Platforms Framework
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: CCFLA’s Urban-Inclusive Country Platforms Framework provides guidance on how a nationally led platform can be designed t...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: CCFLA’s Urban-Inclusive Country Platforms Framework provides guidance on how a nationally led platform can be designed to systematically integrate cities and other subnational actors into climate finance and implementation systems. The framework is built around the barriers that often keep urban priorities out of country platforms – misalignment between national and subnational priorities, weak project pipelines, limited fiscal capacity and creditworthiness, and the absence of city-focused instruments – and responds with a phased roadmap from initial engagement to program readiness, investment programming, financing and implementation. Implementing the framework by national governments would allow for regular engagement with subnational leaders, inclusion of urban ministries and local representatives in coordination structures, support for local climate action plans and project pipelines, aggregation of smaller urban projects, and use of concessional, blended and de-risking tools through intermediaries such as national development banks and local financial institutions. Click here to know more about the framework.

transferability: Host the national platform within suitable institutions according to the governance context. Depending on the level of decentralization and governance arrangements, the platform may be coordinated by a group public and institutional partners, such as Viable Cities, a ministry-led multi-stakeholder platform such as citiES 2030, or a country-led financing framework that is designed to work across national and subnational levels, as in Tanzania.

Adapt the platform functions and mandates to national priorities and capacities.  Countries can prioritize different functions, from initial engagement and program readiness to investment planning, financing and implementation, and adjust the operations of the platform to match their challenges and ambitions.

Bring cities into the platform through mechanisms that fit the governance system. In settings with high local capacities, city mobilization can be direct, as in Viable Cities’ Climate City Contracts. In less capacitated contexts, city mobilization can be routed through national processes while local governments build their own capacities and frameworks over time and continuously engage the national government through multilevel dialogues, as in Tanzania.

Adopt an iterative, learning-by-doing approach where the prioritized strategies and initiatives could first be tested before a full roll-out, especially in context where institutional capacities are limited, as in Tanzania.
enablingConditions: Strong national leadership mandate, cross-government commitment and durable support from a wider political and social base.
Regular consultation with subnational leaders, sectoral working groups, and clear channels for cities to feed into national planning
Institutional capacity and continuity, including a capable coordinating team, clear roles, and sustained staffing, resources and institutional support over time.
Subnational readiness, including subnational and city-level climate and financial plans, data, and support to develop investable pipelines and integrate climate into budgets
Participation of national and multilateral development banks and the private sector to support through innovative, catalytic and concessional finance.

pathways.title: Intermediary Coordination, Facilitation and Accountability Function
pathways.whatItIs: An intermediary coordination function is a dedicated, trusted unit that helps move multilevel climate commitments from agreement to implementation. It sits between participating institutions and provides shared capacity for analysis, facilitation, strategic alignment, monitoring and learning. Why is it needed: The implementation of climate projects often spans siloed institutions with different mandates, resources and decision cycles. To this end, intermediary coordination functions are needed to avoid siloes, align mandates and help sustain coordination beyond specific projects, programs or funding cycles. They also help create institutional memory by through by enabling recurring coordination, documentation of processes and feedback loops, enabling strong institutional relationships, accountability and progressively improving multilevel climate governance system.

title: Jointly Prioritize, Plan and Prepare Investment Portfolios
description: This section will include guidance and tools to support national, subnational and city governments in jointly planning climate investments, preparing projects and developing coordinated urban climate investment pipelines.
systemsLogic: Climate-related investment planning, portfolio development and project preparation are linked steps in turning shared priorities into investment-ready pipelines. Joint investment planning helps identify investments priorities, portfolio development bundles the projects and related governance, regulatory and policy measures into a coherent package; and project preparation facilities then help project pipelines become bankable. Across all of this, coordination, orchestration and technical assistance are what keep the portfolio moving and reduce fragmentation across levels of government.

pathways.title: Joint Climate Investment Planning and Budgeting
pathways.whatItIs: Investment planning and budgeting are complementary activities that provide a recurring process through which national, subnational and city governments can translate shared climate goals into investment priorities, sequencing, responsibilities and indicative resource requirements. Joint investment planning helps identify which climate investments are required, who is expected to deliver and finance them, when they should occur, and how funding gaps and risks will be addressed. Once the investments are identified and planned, climate budgeting then involves integrating priority projects into operating and capital budgets of a municipality or higher levels of government, assigning implementation responsibilities and tracking delivery through the regular budget cycles. When undertaken jointly by national, subnational and local governments, these activities can help align local investment needs with national policies, funding programmes and fiscal decisions – strengthening coordinated climate action across levels of government.

pathways.whyItIsNeeded: Climate action plans may often set out actions without a clear understanding of their costs, financing responsibilities or links to regular budget decisions, which may contribute to the planning-to-investment gap faced by climate projects. Joint climate investment planning and budgeting can therefore help align priorities across levels of government, identify financing needs and gaps and embed agreed investments into routine operating and capital budgets so that climate commitments are translated into coordinated implementation.
keyActors: National and subnational finance and planning ministries or departments; city finance and sector departments; utilities and public agencies; and other private and community actors responsible for funding or delivering priority investments.

illustrativeExamples.title: Climate City Contracts investment planning approach
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Climate City Contracts investment planning approach. The climate investment-planning component of Sweden’s Climate City ...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Climate City Contracts investment planning approach. The climate investment-planning component of Sweden’s Climate City Contracts involves four key steps: 1) develop a city-level emissions and climate risks baseline and make forecasts, 2) identify climate actions that could help lower emissions and climate risks, 3) develop an implementation roadmap for identified climate actions and 4) identify which projects will be funded by public budgets and where additional financing will be needed; map financing actors and explore innovative financing mechanisms accordingly.

illustrativeExamples.title: Climate City Contract Investment Plan of the Hague
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Climate City Contract Investment Plan of the Hague: The city of the Hague has the ambition to be climate-neutral in 2030...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Climate City Contract Investment Plan of the Hague: The city of the Hague has the ambition to be climate-neutral in 2030. The current budget for climate and transition initiatives totals EUR 198.1 million for the period 2024-2027. The Climate Investment Plan of the Hague identifies its investment baseline and barriers, cross-references its existing municipal budget with its sectoral climate action priorities, estimates the gap between current allocations and total capital needs, and examines stakeholder shares, financing sources, implementation and investment risks and delivery arrangements. Its plan therefore connects its climate priorities with both the municipal planning and budget cycle and investment beyond the municipality.

illustrativeExamples.title: C40 Climate Budgeting Framework (CBF). The CBF
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: C40 Climate Budgeting Framework (CBF). The CBF helps cities in developing, implementing, and adopting a credible and rob...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: C40 Climate Budgeting Framework (CBF). The CBF helps cities in developing, implementing, and adopting a credible and robust climate budgeting process, setting out guidance for the budgeting process and output. It treats climate budgeting as a recurring governance process that connects climate action plan targets to annual or cyclical delivery plans, covers both operating and capital budgets, requires ownership by the finance function and cross-departmental teams, assigns implementation responsibilities and embeds monitoring and learning into the ordinary budget process. Further guidance by C40 highlights how to get started on a robust and credible climate budget. This includes securing political commitments from the city leadership and using the climate budget to have multilevel dialogues with the national government to support investment into priority projects.

transferability: Adapt to the governance context. Map where the city planning, budgeting and investment authority sits, and tailor the connections between local, regional and national processes accordingly. In more centralized systems, national or regional finance authorities may lead the investment planning and budgeting process while cities may provide locally grounded investment priorities and implementation evidence.

Develop progressively and expand the scope over time. Lower-capacity governments can begin with climate-aligned budget tagging, a priority investment register, and basic mapping of costs, responsibilities and funding gaps. As data and capacity improve, the process can incorporate more advanced investment planning that extends beyond municipal assets to utilities, households, businesses and regional or national infrastructure.
enablingConditions: Sustained political and administrative mandate. National, subnational and city leaders must authorise the investment planning and budgeting processes, connect it to agreed climate goals and sustain it across annual budget and electoral cycles.

Clear roles, responsibilities and decision pathways. Governments need agreement on who identifies, funds, approves, implements and monitors investments—including the respective responsibilities of national, subnational and local authorities and external actors.
Integration into existing financial planning and budgeting processes covering both operational and investment responsibilities

Monitoring, accountability and review. Responsibilities, expenditure and delivery should be monitored through ordinary budget and operational reporting, with findings used to update priorities, funding assumptions and future budgets.

pathways.title: Portfolio and Pipeline Development
pathways.whatItIs: Portfolio and pipeline development involves translating agreed climate priorities into a coordinated portfolio of interventions and progressively identifying and preparing the investible projects that emerge from it. A portfolio can package projects with enabling policy, governance, procurement, capacity and implementation measures around a common mission, through coordination and aggregation across city, regional and national levels. While not every portfolio intervention needs to be investible from the outset, portfolios can generate a pipeline of projects and investment opportunities that can then be prepared for financing. Therefore, portfolios represent a promising approach to crowd in finance and move from investment planning toward implementation.

pathways.whyItIsNeeded: A project-by-project approach is often insufficient to scale climate investment and implementation. Countries and cities need a portfolio of interventions, with a pipeline of well-prepared projects, integrated with enabling regulations, governance functions, procurement, financing and implementation pathways. This can help turn individual initiatives into a well-connected, sequenced and bankable package of interventions. This way, a portfolio approach could make the path from concepts to implementation clearer and more visible for financiers and investors.
keyActors: private sector and civil society partners

illustrativeExamples.excerpt: System Demonstrators provide a systematic way for governments and funders to move beyond individual projects toward miss...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: System Demonstrators provide a systematic way for governments and funders to move beyond individual projects toward mission-driven urban transition portfolios. Rather than starting with a predefined list of projects, participating cities define a shared mission, map the system and structural barriers, convene relevant public, private and civic actors, and develop a coordinated portfolio of interventions across areas such as governance, infrastructure, regulation, procurement, finance, behaviour and technology. Not every intervention needs to be commercially investible; through implementation and learning, the portfolio can progressively surface projects and wider investment opportunities that are ready to move into project preparation and financing pipelines. In Lund, for example, a broader energy and mobility portfolio helped identify local energy systems as an emerging investment area, with EnergyNet representing one opportunity for further financing and implementation.

illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Project Preparation Facilities (PPFs) are organizations, initiatives, or institutions that support cities in developing ...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Project Preparation Facilities (PPFs) are organizations, initiatives, or institutions that support cities in developing bankable, investment-ready projects, typically from a project’s concept, design, or scoping stage up to the financial close. A PPF may provide technical and/or financial support. PPFs can provide a wide range of support depending on a project’s stage and sector. The overarching goal of PPFs is preparing bankable, or investment-ready, projects. A project is bankable, whether from public or private sources, when its risk-return profile meets investors’ criteria. Key criteria include the probability of success, sufficient estimated cash flows to cover costs and produce returns that meet investor expectations, and whether the project will be implemented by a creditworthy entity.

illustrativeExamples.excerpt: SOURCE is a project-preparation software platform. A joint initiative of the multilateral development banks coordinated ...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: SOURCE is a project-preparation software platform. A joint initiative of the multilateral development banks coordinated by the not-for-profit Sustainable Infrastructure Foundation, SOURCE uses standardised, sector-specific question sets covering the full project lifecycle—aligned with the SDGs and the Paris Agreement—to help governments define, develop and manage sustainable infrastructure projects consistently and transparently, with the aim of improving bankability, crowding in private finance and strengthening public-sector capacity. Its functionality includes portfolio and project monitoring dashboards, document and task management, consistency checks, a Project Preparation Facilities Finder and a public pipeline for project promotion, and it is used in more than 50 countries, including many CHAMP endorsers. The case demonstrates how a shared digital tool can standardise and de-risk project preparation across governments while linking prepared projects to preparation facilities and financiers. illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Findeter’s Sustainable and Competitive Cities Program provides technical assistance and funding to small and intermediar...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Findeter’s Sustainable and Competitive Cities Program provides technical assistance and funding to small and intermediary cities in Colombia to prepare long-term roadmaps to develop and access financing for infrastructure and service projects. The program has supported the diagnostic and structuring phases of projects such as Fusagasugá’s public-lighting modernisation, helping lower preparation and financing risk before investment is mobilized. Findeter’s facility is used predominantly by intermediary cities. As a GCF-accredited entity, Findeter has a national footprint of 2,220 financed projects across 773 municipalities and 30 departments, demonstrating how a national intermediary can help crowd in capital for subnational climate investment at scale. To know more about Findeter, click here.

transferability: Tailor portfolio development to the national climate priorities and implementation capacities. Cities with relatively less capacities can start with mapping key actors, identifying and aligning projects with national priorities, and engaging with key actors, such as PPFs, then move to portfolio development and governance once the actors are involved and enabling conditions are mature.

Different lead institutions can host the portfolio and pipeline development. Depending on the governance setup, portfolio development and coordination role can sit within a national program or agency, regional authority, a multistakeholder body of local governments or external partners, such as city networks. The key is having sufficient mandate and convening power to continually develop and implement the portfolio.

Portfolio funding models can vary. Some contexts will need a donor-led or grant-led portfolio development, while others with higher levels of fiscal capacity can use city-led, national-led or blended funding arrangements. The key is having funding that is sufficient to develop the portfolio from planning to investment readiness.

Tailor outreach to PPFs to match sector priorities, country context and pipeline maturity, so early-stage projects are steered toward diagnostics and concept development, while more advanced pipelines are matched with structuring, de-risking and investment-readiness support.
enablingConditions: A clear mission, mandate and a coordination function. The portfolio needs a national-level mandate (e.g., through a national mission), alongside clear roles across levels of government and an intermediary team or similar coordination function to keep actors, including governments, project developers and financiers coordinated, track progress and revise the portfolio as conditions change.
National-local coordination mechanisms that allow city-level priorities and lessons to feed into national policy, investment programmes and funding decisions.
An investment plan or preliminary pipeline to work from, so the portfolio is built from agreed climate priorities across levels of government, rather than from siloed projects.
Early engagement with project preparation facilities, so that the portfolio and pipeline are prepared for bankability from the outset.

Reliable data and assessment capacity. Governments need sufficient data and technical capacity to identify projects across levels of government, assess readiness, identify gaps and structure a coherent theory of change across the portfolio.

title: Mobilize Finance, Shape Local Markets and Deliver Investment Portfolios
description: This section will include guidance and tools for national, subnational and city governments to mobilize and deploy catalytic funding to test and scale solutions, de-risking mechanisms to support urban climate projects and shape local markets using aggregated procurement.
systemsLogic: Implementing portfolios and pipelines often requires interconnected financing, implementation and market-shaping mechanisms operating together as part of a system. Catalytic and de-risking finance mechanisms can help mobilize investment, while systemic portfolio implementation environments and local climate investment structures and collaborative implementation environments can support coordinated delivery of investments. Procurement complements financing by creating credible demand conditions that allow new solutions to move from demonstrations and small-scale deployment toward wider commercial adoption.

pathways.title: Locally Anchored Multilevel Climate Finance Structures
pathways.whatItIs: Multilevel climate finance structures can be understood as a range of financing arrangements that help municipalities mobilize and deploy capital for climate and transition investment, in collaboration with other levels of government and the private sector. This could include pooled municipal borrowing facilities, trust funds, special purpose vehicles for projects requiring off-balance sheet financing, blended finance arrangements etc. Their purpose is to create a local mechanism for cities to mobilize and deploy climate finance from diverse sources, including national governments, donors or private financiers.

illustrativeExamples.title: Kenya’s County Climate Change Funds (CCCFs)
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Kenya’s County Climate Change Funds (CCCFs) demonstrate how devolved climate finance can enable locally led adaptation w...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Kenya’s County Climate Change Funds (CCCFs) demonstrate how devolved climate finance can enable locally led adaptation while remaining anchored in national policy. CCCFs were piloted in Isiolo in 2011–12 and later expanded to Garissa, Kitui, Makueni, Wajir and beyond. These funds identify, prioritize and finance local adaptation investments through county planning and budgeting systems, with county and ward committees steering decisions and local knowledge and climate information built into planning and monitoring. They are designed to blend resources from international climate finance, multilateral development banks, the private sector, national government transfers and county own-source budgets, and several counties have legislated commitments of 1–2 per cent of development budgets to capitalise the fund. This domestic commitment helped attract external finance, including seed funding from the UK and Sweden and a proposal to the Green Climate Fund to expand the model. The model is aligned with Kenya’s National Adaptation Plan (NAP), the National Climate Change Action Plan, and the Climate Change Act. The success of pilots helped pave the way for national scale-up – by 2023 all 47 Kenyan counties had CCCFs in place, creating the basis for a new Financing Locally-Led Climate Action Program funded by the World Bank and the governments of Denmark and Sweden, and led by the National Treasury.

illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Milan for Trees Fund is a locally led trust fund managed by the municipality of Milan and is dedicated to tree planting ...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Milan for Trees Fund is a locally led trust fund managed by the municipality of Milan and is dedicated to tree planting in the city. The fund is capitalized through a blend of municipal tax revenues, individual contributions and larger corporate donations. The money is held off the municipal balance sheet, and the fund allows tree planting to extend beyond public land. In 2024, 600 citizens and 36 local business participated to raise over EUR 1.3 million to plant over 4700 trees. It is a good example of how a city can lead local multi-stakeholder partnerships, bringing in private capital to fund place-based climate action. The city of Lund in Sweden is also planning to replicate this model to accelerate municipal tree planting, which will not only improve local climatic conditions but also provide additional economic value to businesses through place-based improvements.

illustrativeExamples.title: LoCAL
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: LoCAL is a country-based mechanism spearheaded by the UN Capital Development Fund (UNCDF) It helps local governments int...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: LoCAL is a country-based mechanism spearheaded by the UN Capital Development Fund (UNCDF) It helps local governments integrate climate adaptation into planning and budgeting through performance-based climate resilience grants and technical and capacity-building support. It channels climate finance to local governments through existing national fiscal transfer systems. In practice, local governments assess risks and needs, prepare adaptation plans, identify and budget priority measures, and implement them through their annual budgeting cycles; performance reviews and audits then inform future allocations. LoCAL is designed to scale in phases, moving from piloting to learning and then to full national roll-out, which makes it a strong example of a multilevel local climate finance structure embedded in national systems. Since 2011, LoCAL has provided USD 8.3 million in grants to 64 local governments, impacting over 5 million people across 12 countries in Asia (Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Lao PDR and Nepal), the Pacific (Tuvalu) and Africa (Benin, Ghana, Mali, Mozambique, Niger and Tanzania).

illustrativeExamples.title: Tamil Nadu Water and Sanitation Pooled Fund
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Tamil Nadu Water and Sanitation Pooled Fund illustrates how a dedicated special purpose vehicle can connect municipal pr...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Tamil Nadu Water and Sanitation Pooled Fund illustrates how a dedicated special purpose vehicle can connect municipal projects with state, national and private finance. Established by the Government of Tamil Nadu as a separate trust, the Fund pooled the borrowing needs of 13 small and medium-sized municipalities and issued a single bond to raise long-term capital for water and sanitation investments. Participating municipalities repaid the Fund through project and local revenues, while the state government strengthened the structure through reserve funds and the ability to intercept fiscal transfers if repayments fell short; a USAID partial guarantee provided additional protection to investors.  By ring-fencing the financing and repayment arrangements, the SPV spread risk, reduced transaction costs and enabled municipalities that could not issue bonds independently to access capital markets. The national government subsequently embedded this approach in its national Pooled Finance Development Fund, through which the central government supports state-level pooled finance entities with project-preparation assistance and credit enhancement. The case shows how national and state governments can establish an intermediary SPV that aggregates local investment needs and mobilizes private capital while municipalities retain responsibility for project delivery and repayment.
